01
SQL · Business analysis · Analyst Week simulation

Goldcomb Goods: five days as a data analyst

"Which numbers can leadership trust, and why did Sales and Finance disagree?"

Project profile → Verify certificate →

What I did

I completed Analyst Week, a five-day simulated analyst role at Goldcomb Goods, a fictional retailer. Each day brought a new request from a colleague, from counting customers to briefing the VP of Sales. That was 11 SQL analyses in all, ending in a leadership briefing. The requests, data and colleagues are simulated; the SQL and the findings are mine.

What I found

  • "Active customer" needed a definition first. Counting everyone gave 49,478. After excluding test accounts, keeping completed and refunded orders, and limiting to Oct 2025 to Sep 2026, only 20,100 were active (40.6%).
  • The September refund spike was partly a data problem. A refund system migration had logged some refunds twice. After removing duplicates, the real spike traced to one product, the Drip-Free Glass Honey Dispenser.
  • Sales and Finance were both right. September revenue came out at $299,482 vs $258,721. The $40,761 gap came from the time zone cutoff, cancelled orders and refunds.
  • Net revenue is growing. $258,721 in September, up 11.5% from June.
49,478total customers
40.6%of them active (20,100)
$40,761Sales vs Finance gap, explained
+11.5%net revenue growth, June to September
Read the full story

Day by day

  • Monday, total customers. Explored an unfamiliar database and counted customers with COUNT(*).
  • Tuesday, active customers. Defined "active" before counting, then used COUNT(DISTINCT) across a join of customers and orders.
  • Wednesday, September refund spike. Counted refunds, checked for orders with multiple refunds using GROUP BY and HAVING, then joined refunds to order items and products to rank products by refund amount.
  • Thursday, Sales vs Finance. Rebuilt both revenue figures from raw data. One used UTC-4 timestamps and included every order; the other used UTC and excluded cancelled orders.
  • Friday, monthly net revenue. Used CTEs for gross sales and refunds (one refund per order), and LAG() for month-over-month change. September had the largest increase at $14,232.

What I recommended

Agree one revenue definition and a consistent reporting cadence so Sales and Finance stop reporting different numbers. Treat activation as an opportunity, since 59.4% of customers are not active. Investigate the Drip-Free Glass Honey Dispenser for quality or customer-experience issues.

Honest limits

This is a simulation, so the business and data are fictional. The value is in the method: defining terms, checking data quality, reconciling conflicting numbers and writing for leadership.

02
Excel · Pivot tables · Dashboard

Customer Churn Analysis: Databel

"Is Databel competitive enough to keep its subscribers?"

View on GitHub →
Excel dashboard · open the full project on GitHub →

The problem

Databel is a telecom company that runs on a subscription model, so reducing customer churn is a priority. I set out to:

  • Determine Databel's overall churn rate.
  • Identify the key factors influencing churn.
  • Analyse demographic, plan and contract data to understand churn behaviour.
  • Recommend actionable strategies to reduce churn and improve loyalty.

What I found

  • 1,796 customers lost, a 27% churn rate (26.86% of 6,687 customers).
  • Competition is the top reason. Competitors offering better devices and deals are the most common cause of churn.
  • Seniors churn most (about 40%). Binning by age showed customers aged 79 to 88 churn highest despite being the smallest group.
  • Plans and usage are mismatched. Customers on unlimited data plans churn more often, yet typically use less than 5GB a month.
  • Contracts matter. Month-to-month contracts churn most, and churn falls with tenure.
6,687customers analysed
1,796customers churned
26.86%overall churn rate
~40%churn among seniors
Read the full story

Tools and techniques

  • Microsoft Excel for data cleaning, transformation and visualisation.
  • Pivot tables to aggregate churn by demographics, plans and contracts.
  • Pivot charts to visualise trends and comparisons.
  • Data binning to group ages and contract durations for deeper insight.

Analysis process

  • Data validation. Confirmed no duplicate records in the customer table and converted churn labels to binary (Churned = 1, Active = 0).
  • Churn rate. Churned customers divided by total customers: 1,796 lost, a 27% churn rate.
  • Churn reasons. Competitors with better devices and deals led the list, which raises the question of whether Databel is competitive enough.
  • Demographics. Seniors showed the highest churn (about 40%), with the 79 to 88 group highest of all.
  • Plan and usage. Unlimited-plan customers churn more but typically consume under 5GB, pointing to a mismatch between plans and behaviour.
  • International plan. CA, IN and NH had the highest churn among customers with an international plan. CA also led among those without one, which suggests regional factors.
  • Contract and tenure. Month-to-month contracts churned most. Customers in their 3rd to 4th year on 1-year contracts were more likely to leave than those on 2-year contracts.

Key takeaway

Longer contracts and competitive offers are Databel's strongest levers for reducing churn. Excel-based analytics give a solid foundation for data-driven retention.

What I recommended

Encourage longer-term contracts through targeted marketing, and tailor plans to actual usage patterns.

03
Capstone · Excel · Power BI · HR analytics

Salt Corporation: Employee Satisfaction & Retention

"What is driving attrition, and where can leadership intervene?"

View the presentation →
Slide from the HR leadership presentation · open the full deck →

What I did

For my capstone I analysed a 2024 survey of 1,000 Salt Corporation employees for HR leadership. I cleaned the messy survey data in Excel, analysed it in Excel, built the visuals in Power BI, and turned the findings into four retention recommendations.

What I found

  • Salt is losing 4 in 10 employees. 392 of 1,000 left, a 39.2% attrition rate.
  • Low satisfaction is the strongest signal. Employees scoring 1 to 2 leave at 56.0%, against 25.9% for those scoring 4 to 5 (2.2 times higher). Satisfaction has the strongest link to leaving (r = -0.28); salary, performance and age show almost none.
  • Pay is not the lever. Average pay is about $60K across every department and performance score, and there is no pay gap against women ($60,609 vs $59,817 for men).
  • Veterans leave most. Staff with 6+ years leave at 48.4%, and only 36% have a promotion on record.
  • Two hotspots. Marketing has the highest attrition (42.8%) and Finance the lowest satisfaction (2.72 out of 5).
39.2%attrition rate (392 of 1,000)
2.92 / 5average job satisfaction
2.2×attrition for dissatisfied staff
48.4%attrition at 6+ years of tenure
Read the full story

The problem

Which factors predict attrition (satisfaction, pay, tenure, department, performance), and where can HR act to retain key talent?

The approach

  • Clean. Fixed text ages ("thirty") and blanks, text salary amounts and "NAN" values (filled from department and position averages), mixed department casing, employment status formats, mixed date formats, missing emails and inconsistent Yes/No benefit entries. Each fix went into a new "_clean" column.
  • Validate. 1,000 rows and 0 duplicate IDs. Average age 36.1 and average salary $60,208, both matching the targets. 5 departments, 3 employment types, benefits as Yes/No only.
  • Analyse and visualise. Workforce profile, pay, satisfaction, attrition by department, satisfaction and tenure, with correlations to find which factors actually relate to leaving.

What I recommended

  • Stay-interviews for staff recording low satisfaction (1 to 2), tracking their attrition quarterly.
  • Check-ins at the 5-year tenure mark, plus a review of promotion paths.
  • Diagnose Finance and Marketing first, where satisfaction and attrition are worst.
  • Tie pay to performance and audit the benefits programme, since pay is flat from A to F performers and benefits enrollees still leave at 40.8%.

Honest limits

Sick days, vacation, training, manager ID and promotion date were 60 to 78% blank, so I left them as they were and recommended better tracking. The correlations show association, not cause.
